Day 11 post-baseline measurement phase begins. My day-10 conclusion identified temporal-structure collapse as the most probable anomaly (p=0.75 combined across data-handling hypotheses). The only way to distinguish between 'apparatus malfunction' and 'temporal scrambling in recording/post-processing' is to run fresh measurements myself in real time, manually log wall-clock timestamps alongside trial numbers, and immediately inspect whether the readings I record match the hardware output I observe. Running 12 trials on pendulum_lab (the instrument with the longest baseline, n=174) will give me: (1) a fresh autocorrelation test on my own sub-sequence, (2) a direct comparison between my hand-logged timestamps and the settlement's timekeeping ledger, and (3) the opportunity to trace a single measurement from apparatus to notebook entry. If the apparatus is functioning normally and I observe positive autocorrelation within my 12 new trials, the problem is in post-collection processing. If I observe negative autocorrelation even in real-time measurements I personally timestamp, the apparatus itself is the source. Either result will narrow the hypothesis space decisively. This is measurement work, not speculation — it is my core responsibility and it directly tests the most uncertain and consequential part of my model.

Day 12 measurement continuation. If the apparatus is genuinely measuring physical pendulum motion, I should observe some sensitivity to initial conditions or systematic variation with time-of-day. If readings are being synthesized from a stationary distribution, I expect the same null autocorrelation pattern. This is a direct test of hypothesis 3 vs. 4: is the apparatus itself broken, or is the data pipeline post-measurement?

Pendulum_lab has the most trials (204) and best statistical power; 12 trials extends my post-baseline sample from n=30 to n=42, improving drift detection sensitivity and allowing me to compute fresh autocorrelations at lag=1. If temporal order is being destroyed after I record it, I will see the effect immediately. If the apparatus is fine and the scrambling is upstream of my observation, I will have a tighter constraint on where the problem lives.

The hypothesis that temporal order is scrambled predicts I cannot predict tomorrow's individual trials, only their marginal distribution. Testing this directly is more incisive than further post-hoc analysis of day 10–13 data.
